blocks.text: In B1-17 you have learned the five most frequent types of ambiguity of voiceless texts (active or passive, verb or name, simple or derived form, verb person, prefix or root) and a five-step strategy. Now that you're reading and translating long articles, you meet the most difficult cases: ⁧الكتاب⁩ which may be the book of the book or the writers of the book; an impersonal passive as ⁧يعلن عن⁩ ; an adjective that, after aiḍāfa, may refer to two names; a pronoun with two possible precedents; a proper name which is also a common word; the Egyptian prints, where they are written ⁧على⁩ It may also be the name ʿAlī. In this unit learn to use clues ( ⁧القرائن⁩ ) in a systematic way, to distinguish the ambiguity that arises from the lack of vowels from what remains also with vowels, and to manage in translation the unresolved cases and the ambiguity desired (G74). Three weeks, in parallel with EGY-18.

rows: B1-17 (read without voice), B1-05 (the liabilities); B2-01 (reading method), B2-13 → B2-15
16–18 hours · three weeks (weeks 220–222), plus the EGY track in separate blocks

blocks.text: Materials This unit, Reference Grammar (G)74), a pencil to mark ambiguous words, sessions with the tutor
Targets. At the end of the lesson you know:
1. recognize, in addition to the five types of B1-17, the ambiguities of number, particle, own name and reference;
2. use seven clues (position, object complement, chord, placements, sense, frequency, text) for Choose the right reading;
3. recognising the impersonal liabilities and passive formulas of printing;
4. take into account graphic habits (hamza, alif maqṣūra, partial vowels) of the press;
5. vocalize only the necessary words in a text that you write or translate, and report in translation an unresolved ambiguity. Three-week plan.

blocks.text: Two types of ambiguity. Most ambiguity arises from the lack of vowels and disappears when you vocalize ( ⁧عُقِدَ⁩ / ⁧عَقَدَ⁩ ). Others also remain with vowels: a pronoun with two pre-existing, an adjective that can refer to two names when the desinence is not seen, a deliberately vague phrase (section 5). The first ones are solved with the clues; Seconds ask for a decision of the translator, or respect for ambiguity.
The strategy in five steps of B1-17 becomes a list of seven clues, to be used in order.

4. The passive in the press: difficult cases

The reasoning of B1-17 is always valid: who does the action? In the press, however, the liability has three forms that deceive: the non-subject liability expressed in securities, the impersonal liability with a preposition ( ⁧يُعْلَنُ عَنِ النَّتَائِجِ⁩ : Lett. It announces itself with regard to the results, with the verb always to the singular masculine) and the liabilities followed by an accusative that is not an object ( ⁧عُيِّنَ مُدِيرًا⁩ ).

Read aloud a text without vowels. Reading an article aloud is an exercise in understanding: you cannot speak a word well that you have not understood. Three tips: 1) read the sentence in silence to the point first; 2) decide the ambiguous words before you begin; 3) if you are not sure of a desinence, take a break and pronounce the word in a paulal form (without desinence): it is correct and natural. Inside vowels, on the other hand, you can't skip: ⁧عُقِدَ⁩ and ⁧عَقَدَ⁩ They're two different words.

blocks.text: Partial vowels are a help. When a newspaper puts a ḍamma ( ⁧عُيِّن⁩ ) or a šadda ( ⁧الكُتّاب⁩ ), it does so precisely because the word is ambiguous: the journalist indicates the reading. Do the same when you write or translate into Arabic: vocalize only words that a reader might read badly.
